historical_timeline.summary: Born in Oakville, Alabama, to a sharecropping family.
Nearly dies of pneumonia at about 7, in an epidemic in which a brother and a sister die; the family soon moves to Cleveland.
National interscholastic records; enters the Ohio State University, where he is barred from the dormitory because of his race.
Four gold medals at the Berlin Olympic Games.
Files for personal bankruptcy after a business fails; years of hardship and exclusion follow the Games.
Moves with his wife from Chicago to the Phoenix area.
Presidential Medal of Freedom; a pack-a-day smoker for decades.
Admitted in Chicago with shortness of breath; inoperable adenocarcinoma of the left lung diagnosed; chemotherapy in Chicago and Tucson.
Dies of lung cancer in Tucson at 66.

claims.statement: James Cleveland (J.C.) Owens was born on September 12, 1913, in Oakville, Alabama, the youngest of the children of Henry and Mary Emma Owens, who were sharecroppers. The Ohio State University Libraries give ten children; contemporary newspaper accounts and his own account give nine.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented date used for the synthetic date of birth. The number of children differs between sources and is recorded as given.

source_links.locator: born Sept. 12, 1913 ... the last of 10 children raised by Henry and Mary Emma Owens ... sharecroppers

roster birth date

claims.statement: As a child in Alabama he worked in the fields with his family. At about 7 he had pneumonia and nearly died; a brother and a sister died during the same epidemic. He later described himself as a sickly, emaciated, poverty-stricken child, and said that his parents knew the family had to leave to survive. In the early 1920s the family moved north to Cleveland, following an older sister who had written home about jobs there.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own published account, repeated in contemporary newspaper obituaries, with the move dated by the Ohio State University Libraries. Anchors the past medical history (childhood pneumonia) and the family history.

source_links.locator: When he was 7 years old, he contracted pneumonia and nearly died. A brother and sister did die during the epidemic; the sickly, emaciated J.C.; the sickly, poverty-stricken kid from Oakville
By the early 1920s ... Lillie had moved north to Cleveland ... So, the Owens family moved to Cleveland

claims.statement: In Cleveland a teacher misheard his initials J.C. and called him Jesse, and the name stuck. Coached by Charles Riley from junior high school, he won the long jump, set a world record in the 220-yard dash and tied the world record in the 100-yard dash at the National Interscholastic Championship in 1933.

source_links.locator: one of his teachers, misinterpreting how he pronounced J.C. ... started calling him Jesse; National Interscholastic Championship in Chicago

claims.statement: At the Ohio State University, which he entered in 1933, he was barred from the men's dormitory because of his race, lived in a boarding house with other African American students, and could not eat in the restaurants along High Street. He worked as a freight elevator operator. At the Big Ten championships in May 1935 he set world records in the 220-yard dash, the 220-yard low hurdles and the long jump.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented racial discrimination in his education; it anchors the social history and the plan's attention to equity.

source_links.locator: Owens was barred from it because of his race ... No restaurant along High Street would serve them; By May 1935 ... set world records in the 220-yard dash, the 220-yard low hurdles and the long jump
I was running a freight elevator 12 hours a week

claims.statement: At the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin he won four gold medals, in the 100 meters, the 200 meters, the long jump and the 4 x 100-meter relay, and he was given a ticker-tape parade in New York on his return.

source_links.locator: four gold medals, in the 100 and 200-meter dashes, the 400 meter relay and the broad jump; won the 100-meters in 10.3, 200-meters in 20.7 and the long jump

claims.statement: The offers that followed the Games did not become steady work. He earned money racing against horses and local sprinters, and said that Black athletes were not allowed in any professional sport then. A dry-cleaning business he founded in 1938 went into debt, and he filed for personal bankruptcy in 1939. He owed taxes on his income after the Games, and decades later was in trouble with the Internal Revenue Service again for failing to file returns. He later worked through public relations firms, as a speaker, and with youth organizations.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented years of financial hardship and racial exclusion after the Games. Anchors the modern social history (speaking and youth work) and the plan's attention to cost and access.

claims.statement: He met Minnie Ruth Solomon at Fairmount Junior High School in Cleveland in 1930; they married and had three daughters. In the early 1970s, with their children grown, they moved from Chicago, their home of more than 20 years, to the Phoenix area of Arizona. Ruth Owens died in 2001.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern household. His daughters are not named and no relative is given a role or a health fact in the modern episode.

claims.statement: He smoked cigarettes for decades: at his death newspapers described him as a pack-a-day smoker for the past 35 years, and his doctors said he had smoked about a pack a day. The Ohio State University Libraries call him a lifetime smoker.
claims.clinical_interpretation: About 35 pack-years, the figure used for the modern smoking history; it meets the 2021 USPSTF screening threshold of 20 pack-years. The start year is not documented.

claims.statement: He was admitted to Michael Reese Hospital in Chicago on December 12, 1979, after reporting shortness of breath; the illness was diagnosed as adenocarcinoma of the left lung, described as inoperable. He received chemotherapy, was moved when he was able to travel to University Hospital in Tucson, and had outpatient chemotherapy at the University of Arizona Cancer Center, with breathlessness and difficulty talking.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented diagnosis to which the synthetic modern adenocarcinoma of the left upper lobe is linked. In the modern episode the cancer is found by screening at an earlier stage, which is the teaching contrast.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Find lung cancer early in a 65-year-old Black man who has smoked a pack a day for 35 years and who was never offered screening: confirm eligibility on the USPSTF 1974 criteria (50 to 80 years, 20 pack-years or more, smoking now or quit within 15 years), hold the shared decision-making visit with a decision aid and tobacco treatment that the CMS coverage decision requires, read the low-dose CT with Lung-RADS, and work up a category 4X nodule without delay: PET-CT, brain MRI, systematic EBUS staging of the mediastinum (ACCP), and tissue for PD-L1 and comprehensive biomarker testing before any immunotherapy. Then treat resectable stage IIB adenocarcinoma on the NCCN guideline: tumor board review, physiologic evaluation for lobectomy (ACCP), three cycles of nivolumab with carboplatin and pemetrexed before surgery (CheckMate 816), immune-related adverse event monitoring, thoracoscopic lobectomy with lymph node dissection, and surveillance CT; treat tobacco dependence with varenicline even after the diagnosis; and track each step for delay, because Black Americans are less often found eligible for and offered screening and less often offered surgery for early lung cancer.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Owens returns two weeks after the screening CT. PET-CT three days after the scan showed the 2.9 cm left upper lobe nodule and a left interlobar node to be active, with nothing in the mediastinum or elsewhere, and brain MRI the next day was clear. Endobronchial ultrasound a week ago found adenocarcinoma in the interlobar node, with four other node stations negative. PD-L1 is 40 percent, and tissue sequencing, back yesterday, shows a KRAS G12C mutation and no EGFR, ALK or other targetable alteration. The thoracic tumor board reviewed him five days ago. He had pulmonary function tests this morning and saw Dr. Halvorsen-Pierce at midday. He still has his usual morning cough, no breathlessness, and has lost no weight. He is still smoking a pack a day and now wants to stop: the scan has convinced him. He has had no thoughts of self-harm.

assessment_plan.assessment: Non-small cell lung cancer found by his first screening CT while it can still be cured. Systematic EBUS staging shows hilar (N1) but not mediastinal spread, and PET-CT and brain MRI show no metastases. Because there is no EGFR or ALK alteration, nivolumab with platinum chemotherapy before surgery is an option that improves event-free survival and the chance of a complete pathologic response over surgery first, and the tumor board and Dr. Halvorsen-Pierce recommend it. His lung function allows a lobectomy (predicted postoperative FEV1 and DLCO both 63 percent). The KRAS G12C result does not change treatment now, but is kept for any recurrence

assessment.assessment: Question 1: this is lung adenocarcinoma, stage IIB (AJCC 8th edition): a 2.9 cm primary with a positive interlobar node and negative mediastinal stations on systematic EBUS sampling (4R, 4L and 7 plus 10L), as ACCP guidance advises when a hilar node is positive; PET-CT and brain MRI complete the staging, and no mediastinoscopy is needed. Question 2: it is resectable by lobectomy. Because EGFR and ALK are negative, the tumor board recommends three cycles of nivolumab with carboplatin and pemetrexed before surgery (CheckMate 816), which improved event-free survival and the rate of pathologic complete response over surgery alone without making surgery less feasible, then thoracoscopic left upper lobectomy with systematic node dissection. Question 3: EGFR and ALK had to be excluded first, because targeted therapy, not chemoimmunotherapy, would be preferred around surgery if either were present; PD-L1 of 40 percent supports immunotherapy. KRAS G12C does not change treatment for resectable disease but makes sotorasib or adagrasib options if it ever recurs

Question 5: stopping smoking now lowers the risk of complications after surgery and the risk of recurrence and second cancers, and improves survival; it is part of his cancer treatment. Varenicline with counseling is the most effective approach

recommendations: Three cycles of nivolumab 360 mg with carboplatin AUC 5 and pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 every three weeks, starting in about a week; folic acid and vitamin B12 first; dexamethasone around each pemetrexed dose; hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV tests before cycle 1
Restaging CT of the chest and upper abdomen after cycle 3, then thoracoscopic left upper lobectomy with systematic mediastinal and hilar node dissection about five weeks after the last cycle

Question 4: he is fit for lobectomy. Predicted postoperative FEV1 and DLCO are both about 63 percent, above 60 percent, so no exercise test is needed (ACCP). Prehabilitation in a pulmonary rehabilitation program during chemotherapy, and rehabilitation again after surgery

Immune-related adverse event monitoring before each cycle: blood count, TSH, free T4, liver tests, creatinine and glucose, with morning cortisol at baseline and before each infusion; a written list of warning symptoms (new cough or breathlessness, diarrhea, rash, yellowing, severe tiredness or headache) and the 24-hour oncology line
Varenicline from today with a quit date on the day of cycle 1, the quitline, and tobacco review at every visit

After surgery, decide on further treatment from the pathology: with a major pathologic response and negative nodes, surveillance is reasonable, since this regimen was given before surgery only; then chest CT every six months for two to three years and yearly low-dose CT afterwards, with no routine PET-CT, brain MRI or tumor markers

Question 6: primary care to share symptom, mood and distress screening, tobacco support, vaccinations (pneumococcal vaccine before treatment) and the preventive care due at his age. Specialist palliative care is not needed now for a cancer treated with curative intent and causing no symptoms; we will refer if needs arise
